item.title: Therapy in the Age of AI: What We Can Actually Do
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Therapy in the Age of AI: What We Can Actually Do

The profession has a problem. Here is how we can begin to meet it.

Posted July 11, 2026

Key points
  • Some people will prefer a human therapist, but others will prefer AI.
  • The generalist will be more vulnerable, but certain specialities will likely be more protected.
  • Ethical and legal issues remain challenging as we venture into new territory.
  • There are real things we can do, but none are available if we aren't looking honestly at the problem.

In a recent post, I outlined four things the therapy profession is ignoring about its own future. The research on chatbot outcomes, the vulnerability of the 50-minute hour, what we actually ask of our clients, and what competition does to pricing in every market it touches. This is the follow-up I promised: what now?

Source: Image created by ChatGPT

First, Some Honesty About Where I Stand

I love my work, and it has given me real meaning and purpose for 30 years. I have always said I will never retire, and I mean that. I believe deeply in what skilled human therapists offer that AI genuinely cannot replicate.

But I also think we are ignoring something that rarely gets said out loud: therapy is not always a positive experience. I have done my share of my own work over the years, and I do not look back on every therapist I have seen with warmth or gratitude. Some of those experiences were unhelpful. One was worse than that. The idealized version of therapy that our profession projects, the transformative relationship, the healing alliance, is real for many people, but it is not universal, and I think that pretending otherwise does not serve our clients or our credibility.

A Changed World

Some people will always want the experience of being known by another person, of sitting across from someone with a human history and their own losses, who chose this work for reasons that have nothing to do with an algorithm. That is real, and I cannot fathom that it would disappear.

And yet it is also true that some people will always prefer an LLM. This is not a failure of therapy, but a reflection of a changed world. Young people in particular have grown up on AI. For many of them, a chatbot does not feel like a lesser option. It feels familiar, private, and safe in ways that sitting across from a stranger simply does not. We need to make room for that reality rather than dismiss it. But "some clients will always prefer us" is not an effective strategy with which to meet the future. It is a comfort, and right now, comfort is not what this moment requires.

Where AI Genuinely Falls Short

Understanding where AI struggles is not just reassuring, it is strategically important. The clinicians who develop genuine expertise in the areas where AI is weakest will probably be the ones best positioned going forward.

Couples work is a good example. AI platforms are sycophantic. They are designed to be agreeable, to validate, to avoid conflict so as to maintain engagement. That is a significant liability in couples therapy, where the work often requires holding two contradictory realities simultaneously, challenging both partners, and tolerating the discomfort of not taking sides. An AI that tells each partner what they want to hear is not doing couples therapy and could easily make things worse. The same is true of psychedelic-assisted therapy, which requires a depth of human presence and clinical judgment that no algorithm can provide.

Crisis intervention is another area of concern. Large language models can produce responses that sound reasonable but lack the common sense and real-time situational judgment that crisis work requires. They cannot read a room, hear a change in tone, soothe a parent, or make the kind of split-second clinical judgment a human therapist makes when someone is in genuine danger.

Cultural sensitivity is also a significant challenge. These algorithms are trained on data that reflects the biases of whoever produced it. Clients from underrepresented communities may find that AI responses miss their cultural context. A therapist who has done cultural competency work brings critical knowledge to that relationship, no current model can replicate.

What We Can Do

Knowing where AI falls short points directly toward where I believe therapists should invest. Deepening skills in couples work, crisis intervention, trauma, cultural competency, and complex family systems is not just good clinical practice. It is a good professional strategy.

AI literacy is also becoming essential. This means knowing how to ask clients about their AI use, how to assess whether it is helping or harming, and how to have informed conversations about what these tools can and cannot do. Clients are already using AI for mental health support, often without mentioning it. The therapist who knows how to bring that into their therapy room is offering something genuinely valuable.

There are also real opportunities to work thoughtfully in conjunction with AI, essentially offering your clients the best of both AI and human therapies. Customized relaxation and mindfulness tools can be tailored to a client and used between sessions, extending the work without extending the clinical hour. Therapy apps can provide between-session support. Virtual reality offers new possibilities for exposure work and trauma processing, with the therapist guiding and integrating the experience. The therapists who learn to use these tools thoughtfully will be offering a richer model of care and a more competitive one.

A Note on Ethics and Liability

This is genuinely new territory, and the law has not caught up with the technology. Different states have different rules about informed consent, therapy bots, and liability when AI is part of the treatment. If something goes wrong, the liability will stay with us.

As such, we need to proceed thoughtfully, document carefully, and stay current with the legal landscape in our states. We are forging a new path, and while that is genuinely exciting, it also means watching our backs. Ethical and legal mistakes can be so costly, and our professional associations have not all caught up with the guidance necessary to help us move forward. Nonetheless, AI tools and hybrid therapy models are improving rapidly and cost a fraction of what human therapy costs. That pressure is not going away. The therapists who navigate it best will be the ones making thoughtful decisions now rather than hoping the problem resolves itself.

We Are Not Alone in This

Of course, most if not all professions are experiencing their own versions of these pressures, and many people are scared. Yet I believe we are unusually well equipped to meet this moment. We have spent our careers learning to sit with uncertainty, to tolerate not knowing, and to help others move through fear toward something more workable. That is exactly what this moment asks of us.

Let's stop with the "AI won't replace your job," and rise to this occasion. It is only in doing so that we will be able to be midwives for the future, instead of relics of a different time.

item.title: Fixing Remote Work Behaviors That Wouldn't Fly In Person
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Fixing Remote Work Behaviors That Wouldn't Fly In Person

Why teams require professional self-control rather than raw authenticity.

Posted July 11, 2026

Key points
  • Digital communication layers strip away the sensory guardrails that naturally regulate human behavior.
  • Virtual meeting tools offer bad actors plausible deniability for cruel or dismissive behaviors.
  • Evolutionary psychology suggests healthy group disapproval is an essential tool for behavioral regulation.
  • Effective teams do not require complete authenticity; they require a shared standard of best behavior.

Remote work was sold as the ultimate escape from the annoyances of sharing a physical space with other people during working hours. No more micromanagers hovering over your shoulder, and no more exhausting watercooler gossip.

But there is a dark side to remote work. Remote environments have not cured counterproductive behavior, and they have stripped away some of the social guardrails that keep malicious and destructive colleagues in check.

Although a screen makes it easy to temporarily dodge a destructive coworker, avoiding the person also means avoiding the confrontation required to stop them. This has the potential to create an accountability vacuum. Rather than being challenged or corrected, manipulative people can get away with far more when they can hide behind their screens.

The Virtual Weaponization of Rudeness

In a physical meeting room, human behavior tends to be kept reasonably civil by a shared sensory environment. Bad manners carry an immediate, painful social cost.

If a colleague talks over you, ignores you, or rolls their eyes in a physical meeting room, the entire room sees the hostility. People quickly check the reactions of others to understand if their colleagues are seeing the same behavior and interpreting it in the same way. There’s a shared understanding of the social reality that comes across differently in shared physical spaces.

Crossing your arms defensively, sighing heavily, or engaging in a blatant side conversation requires a massive amount of overt, aggressive confidence. The physical presence of your peers creates social accountability, forcing people to regulate their impulses.

Virtual meetings completely shatter these guardrails. On a video call, rude behavior is compartmentalized and stripped of context when people are in their separate little boxes on screen.

When isolated incidents harden into a chronic, unaddressed pattern of undermining others, the technology becomes an ideal camouflage for several distinct types of workplace disrespect.

1. Muted Laughs

In a physical room, bursting out laughing while a colleague is speaking is an overt act of social aggression that instantly halts the meeting. On a video call, however, bad actors can actively laugh, smirk, or scoff while hitting the mute button. Because the audio doesn’t interrupt others, the behavior is easily shrugged off as a minor digital distraction. A presenter can be left watching someone visibly mock them in real time, while the rest of the room assumes the person is just reacting to a private message. The technology provides a layer of plausible deniability for cruelty.

2. Digital Interruptions

In a physical workspace, interrupting someone repeatedly creates a jarring, uncomfortable social experience that tends to mark the interrupter as aggressive. On a video call, constant interrupting can be disguised by the environment and equipment. Bad actors can cut people off repeatedly, talk over their colleagues, and then casually blame their connection when challenged. Indeed, sometimes people use a poor connection to disrupt conversations and continuously interrupt their colleagues. The tech provides a ready-made excuse for rude or unprofessional behavior.

3. Backchannel Whispers

Whispering to a coworker during a live presentation in a physical office is glaringly obvious and universally considered rude. Online, however, the backchannel is a superpower for bullies. Some people use private Slack messages or personal phones to run a live, invisible commentary during a colleague's presentation, undermining a peer in real time while staring directly at the camera with a polite, fake smile.

4. Continuous Partial Attention

In a shared space, staring blankly out the window or scrolling on your phone while a colleague is speaking to you is deeply insulting and instantly caught. On a video call, people can completely check out. They open another tab, scroll social media, or answer emails while their team members are speaking, weaponizing the digital screen to completely ignore their peers.

To be fair, this is a highly common remote behavior and is rarely malicious if it happens occasionally. Tuning out naturally happens during bloated meetings, at the end of an exhausting day, or when the specific topic under discussion is genuinely irrelevant to that person’s immediate work.

The problem is when this behavior bleeds into critical, shared discussion times. Tuning out important, collective information and then later demanding that colleagues backtrack to re-explain everything that was already covered is where the behavior becomes disruptive. It is social loafing, avoiding the cognitive work of a meeting, effectively offloading the burden of paying attention onto the rest of the team.

The Avoidance Loop

Why don’t we fix this? Because remote work makes it far too easy to choose temporary comfort or avoidance over the difficult task of conflict resolution.

Most people naturally default to conflict avoidance when given the chance. In a shared office, if a colleague is setting out to sabotage your work or insult you, there is more pressure to deal with it when avoidance is not an option.

Online, you can simply close the laptop, mute their notifications, or decline their calendar invite. For a few days or weeks, you may actually forget how unpleasant they are. But this avoidance allows the behavior to continue unchallenged. Managers avoid the awkwardness of a digital confrontation over behavioral nuances that seem difficult to prove, and the damage is done daily, but not all at once to the same people.

The Necessity of Collective Accountability

Anyone who has seen the worst behavior in remote environments run unchecked knows exactly how exhausting this dynamic is. Most people who work remotely will have watched a chaotic colleague run roughshod over a virtual meeting, hiding behind the safety of their screen while the rest of the team sits in their separate spaces, virtually checking out.

Some aspects of contemporary HR culture love to push the cliché of "bringing your true self to work." But sometimes a person's "true self" is lazy, irritable, or completely self-absorbed. In collective spaces that demand productivity, the team doesn't need your true self, they need your best behavior.

Shame gets a bad reputation, but some evolutionary and moral psychologists would argue that it is actually a highly calibrated defense mechanism designed to prevent us from ruining our reputation. Bullying and undermining colleagues are inherently shameful behaviors. When our actions are fully exposed to a physical room, the natural threat of group disapproval triggers this social alarm system, forcing us to self-regulate.

Shared physical environments force a necessary level of psychological and physical self-control. They demand that we restrain our petty impulses, monitor our body language, and actively perform the cooperative, professional version of ourselves.

Visibility is an important part of working together. Flexibility is a brilliant tool for autonomy, but when we completely remove the physical room, we strip away the shared guardrails that keep human behavior civilized.
